title: Capita shares plunge 70% as boss quits after civil service pensions failure
content: Shares in outsourcing business Capita have sunk 70% after its boss stepped down as the saga over public sector pensions drags on. Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has agreed with the firm's board to leave with "immediate effect", admitting that the company had "not delivered" for members of the UK's Civil Service pension scheme. The scheme, which manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK, has been mired in controversy, with tens of thousands of retiring civil servants having faced delays receiving their pension payments. Capita has cut its profit forecast, partly due to the problems surrounding the scheme, and says it plans to raise £190m to bolster its finances. Capita took over the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme in December last year. One Cabinet Office minister last month labelled the company's progress in improving how it runs the scheme as "abysmal". Hernandez, who will be replaced by current chief financial officer Pablo Andres, said: "I am proud of the groundwork we have laid and the progress we have made under my leadership. "Of course, within that I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the Civil Service pension scheme deserve." Capita said it was now expecting its underlying operating profit for 2027 to be hit by between £85m and £95m, having previously expected a reduction of up to £40m. This comes from the extra cost of the recovery plan, as well the loss of two other "major" contracts in the defence and pension solutions divisions. Capita said it was planning an equity raise of £190m in the first half of next year, in order for the company to "move forward from a more stable foundation". The backlog of payments from the civil service pension scheme has been described as "hell" by people who have failed to receive money, some of whom retired early owing to ill health. BBC Radio 4's Money Box programme has been hearing from people caught up in the saga , and left in financial hardship. Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the Public Accounts Committee of MPs, said: "The mishandling of the civil service pension scheme has caused severe hardship for some scheme members, particularly considerably delayed bereavement payments. "The PAC will continue to pursue this dreadful matter and we can only hope that the new acting Chief Executive, Pablo Andres, will be able to get a grip on this whole affair." Until the end of November 2025, the scheme was administered by a company called MyCSP. The contract was taken over by Capita on 1 December, in a seven-year deal worth £239m. "Capita inherited an enormous backlog of cases which needed addressing and failed to deliver on the promised automation, AI and digital tools needed to manage the 1.7 million members," said Russ Mould, investment director at investment platform AJ Bell. "Efforts to fix the problems failed and government deadlines came and went, leading to the withholding of milestone payments, with the National Audit Office probing the contract. "Capita needs to steady the ship quickly, and hope that the modest recent improvements in service levels on the civil service scheme can be built upon."

The 70% plunge in Capita shares and the resignation of its CEO due to the company's failure to deliver on pension scheme management is a substantial and important story that provides a clear reason for readers to care.

title: Faisal Islam: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire
content: There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours around Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive after he admitted an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy. The shock announcement of his return to the chipmaker was followed by the addition of one trillion dollars of stock market value to Nvidia. Then it was the moment President Trump admitted the obvious: that it was his "You're unfired" message direct to the board that changed the decision. The nature of the U-turn is clear from what Nvidia was saying just last week. The board was clear that Huang was not returning. The interim management had also suggested some shifts in strategy away from the Huang era. All of that is now in the dustbin of corporate history. This is a comeback that exceeds the return of Sam Altman to OpenAI or Steve Jobs to Apple, in terms of sheer numbers. The reason for the turnaround was pretty clear in the first statement. The US government had said there were no national security concerns with his reinstatement. Such a reassurance could only have come from the White House. And an hour later President Trump revealed that he had spoken directly to the Nvidia board . This is where I go back to my own conversation with Jensen Huang last September , where he openly advocated for allowing Chinese access to advanced Nvidia microchips. He was one of the few people in the world who could credibly say he knew the minds of both President Trump and President Xi. Reports in the US say there were splits in the Trump administration between China hawks wanting to restrict exports, and others who backed Huang's argument. There is still an independent investigation into the company's compliance with export controls. Nvidia's chips are critical to the development of frontier artificial intelligence systems. Jensen Huang's influence over this pipeline meant he was more important than many world leaders. This is a move of importance not just to the flagging US tech stock boom, but the future of the world economy, of US politics, and of course the geopolitical race between the US and China. The recent doubts about Nvidia struck at the heart of the AI boom. This is after all a company actually generating phenomenal amounts of real sales - over $400bn (£305bn) this year, compared with $27bn four years ago. Nvidia's stock market valuation has been used as a critical form of financing for other companies to construct data centres. A complex web of loans, guarantees, and shareholdings helped spread and sustain the AI boom. Jensen Huang's exit had raised doubts about the fragility of this system, and the interim management had suggested a more "disciplined and selective" approach. The concerns about so-called "circular financing" still raise concerns from some analysts. The public backlash against datacentres and AI evident at the US midterm elections also point to a changed environment. The Democrats in Congress have vowed to investigate both the President and Mr Huang, and he is due to appear before them next week. Jensen Huang is at the centre of it all - the technology, the financing, the US politics and the geopolitics. Today has proven Jensen Huang was in fact, too big to fire.

title: Catering giant to switch main share listing to US in further blow to UK
content: Catering giant Compass Group is planning to switch its primary stock market listing from the UK to the US in a move which will deal another blow to the London Stock Exchange. A source close to the company told the BBC an official announcement was expected to be made in its full-year results on Tuesday. Compass Group is made up of several brands which supply food and drink to various places, ranging from football stadiums and visitor attractions to schools, universities and large corporations. It is understood the proposed shift to the US, which was first reported by the Financial Times , is being made due to the number of investors and the increasing business Compass has across the Atlantic. North America accounts for two-thirds of its business, which drove its total 2025 revenues to $46.1bn. However, such a move would deal a further blow to the London Stock Exchange (LSE), which has seen a growing number of firms leave the UK to list shares in the US in recent years. These include tech firm Arm Holdings, Just Eat, Deliveroo and Paddy Power's parent company Flutter. Long-running speculation also remains over the future of London stalwarts Shell and pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca, which began listing shares in New York in February. Compass describes itself as "possibly the biggest business you've never heard of" due to its plethora of catering and hospitality brands it operates its business under, which include Levy, Bon Appétit, Eurest, Morrison Healthcare and Chartwells. The company was created during the Second World War after the Factories Canteen Order meant large manufacturing or munitions firms employing 250 people or more had an obligation to provide hot meals for workers. Today, Compass operates across more than 25 countries and employs more than 600,000 people. It is understood the group's proposed move to the US will have no impact on the number of UK employees and a consultation process with investors could take more than a year. It is expected to retain a secondary listing in London. In a sign its listing could change, Compass changed the currency in which it trades its standard shares on the LSE from sterling to US dollars in April this year. The boss of the LSE recently called on the government to do more to back homegrown companies and make the UK "more attractive" to invest in the domestic stock market. Dame Julia Hoggett told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the chancellor and the prime minister saying, then let's make sure that we're creating structural incentives to do so. "We need to take the handbrake off." Last year, there were 23 initial public offerings (IPOs) on the London market, with £2.1bn raised. In the US, which has much larger capital markets, there were 354 with $44bn (£33bn) raised.
